A detailed building energy model could help to inform the cost saving potential of each of the following to help prioritize the retrofits. Building management can prioritize retrofits in other ways, though, such as by the cost of installation, occupant comfort and health, life of the existing equipment, and/or the ability of maintenance staff to carry out the retrofit. Some considerations to potentially reduce energy costs are below: • Converting all lighting to efficient LED lamps. For the inside, lighting should match the current LED lamps for consistency of light quality and ease of lamp replacements. • Installing daylight or occupancy sensors for the lighting in the common rooms and laundry areas. Such sensors can dim or shut off lights when there is sunlight coming in through the windows and/or there are no occupants present. • Installing programmable thermostats for common areas with a temperature set back during nighttime hours. • Installing smart parking lot controllers for the head bolt heaters in the parking lot. These controls vary the on/off times for the outlets based on outdoor temperatures, so that in warmer temperatures they are on less often and reduce energy use. • Choosing appliances such as refrigerators, washing machines, and dryers with ENERGY STAR appliances as current appliances reach their end of life will save consumers money. ENERGY STAR appliances achieve the highest performance efficiencies and thus represent options with the lowest operating costs6. • Air sealing and insulating the walls of the crawlspace. This may be feasible from the interior with detailing the vapor barrier around penetrations at the wall boundary and using spray foam or foam board insulation on the walls and in the rim joists (replacing the fiberglass insulation that in some places is compressed or not extending all the way to the edge). However, it is better practice to do from the exterior, excavating around the foundation and adding foam board insulation. Exterior insulation will help keep the interior surfaces warm, so they do not experience condensation. In either case it is important to preserve the crawlspace ventilation. Information about energy retrofits for crawlspaces can be found in the Building America Solution Center (https://basc.pnnl.gov/building-components/crawlspaces). • Replacing the deteriorating siding. That is an ideal time to insulate the building from the exterior. Continuous exterior insulation has other advantages, such as stopping the thermal bridging that occurs through studs and serving as an air barrier to reduce air leakage.
